reasons: No test or other evidence that the page works in use was found in this file.
The project list request does not check the response status, so an error response can break the list.
The 30 second refresh timer starts on load and is never stopped.
The Vue library is loaded without a pinned version, so a new release could change behavior.
Errors are shown only as short messages, with no way to retry.

terms.meaning: a library that updates the page automatically when the app's stored data changes
a styling library that uses short class names to set colors and spacing
a web server that hands out shared library files so the page does not need to host them
a doorway other programs use to ask this app for data
a short pop-up message that appears in a corner and disappears after a few seconds
a Vue way of linking a form field to a stored value so the two stay in step

depends_on: the backend API at the address in apiBaseUrl, using its health route and its projects routes

sections.name: File setup (part 1)
sections.title: Page setup and header bar
sections.what: Sets up the page, loads the Vue and Tailwind libraries, and draws the blue header with the app name and a status badge that shows whether the API is connected. It also draws the row of tab buttons.
sections.why: Likely reason: the header and tabs stay visible on every screen, so the user always sees the connection status and can switch views.
sections.watch_out: The page depends on the internet to load Vue and Tailwind, so without access to those hosts the page appears broken or unstyled.

sections.name: File setup (part 2)
sections.title: Dashboard summary cards
sections.what: Draws three cards on the dashboard: the total number of projects, the number of active projects, and the database type. The counts update from the stored project list.
sections.why: Likely reason: a quick summary lets the owner see the state of the data at a glance.
sections.watch_out: The counts depend on the project list being a real list, so a bad list response would make these cards wrong or fail.

sections.name: File setup (part 3)
sections.title: Quick action buttons on dashboard
sections.what: Draws four large buttons on the dashboard for creating a project, viewing projects, opening the API docs tab, and running a health check.
sections.why: Likely reason: these are shortcuts to the most common actions so the user does not need to use the tab bar.
sections.watch_out: The New Project button also switches to the projects tab, so it changes the screen as well as opening the form.

sections.name: File setup (part 4)
sections.title: New project form
sections.what: Draws the form for creating a project with fields for name, asset type, location, and capacity in megawatts. Submitting it runs the create method, and cancel hides the form.
sections.why: Likely reason: the owner needs one place to enter the basic facts about a new project.
sections.watch_out: The name field is required in the browser, but the capacity field can be left blank and is then sent as empty rather than as a number.

sections.name: File setup (part 5)
sections.title: Projects list header and states
sections.what: Draws the projects section heading, the New Project button, and the messages shown while the list is loading or when there are no projects. It also starts the table that lists projects.
sections.why: Likely reason: users need to know whether the list is still loading or simply empty, instead of seeing a blank table.
sections.watch_out: The New Project button hides while the form is open, so the form can only be closed with its own cancel or close buttons.

sections.name: File setup (part 6)
sections.title: Project table rows and actions
sections.what: Fills the table with one row per project showing its name, asset type, location, status, created date, and View and Delete buttons. Active projects get a green status badge and other statuses get a grey one.
sections.why: Likely reason: each row gives a quick look at the project and the two actions available for it.
sections.watch_out: The Delete button is shown on every row with no role check, so any visitor to the page can remove a project.

sections.name: File setup (part 7)
sections.title: Pop-up messages and starting app data
sections.what: Draws the pop-up message area in the bottom right corner, then starts the app's setup. It sets the backend address, the status values, the tab list, the project list, the new project form values, and the pop-up list.
sections.why: Likely reason: the pop-up area sits outside the tabs so messages appear on any screen, and the starting values give the form and lists a known state.
sections.watch_out: The backend address can be changed by a page parameter, so the page will send requests to whatever address is given there.

sections.name: File setup (part 8)
sections.title: Health check, loading and creating projects
sections.what: Calls the backend health route to set the status badge and database type, then loads the project list from the projects route. It also sends a new project to the backend and, if that works, clears the form and reloads the list.
sections.why: Likely reason: the page needs to know whether the backend is reachable before it shows data, and it reloads the list after a change so the new project appears.
sections.watch_out: The project list fetch does not check whether the response is successful, so an error page or message could be stored as the project list and break the table and counts.

sections.name: File setup (part 9)
sections.title: Deleting, viewing, and auto refresh
sections.what: Asks for confirmation, then deletes a project and reloads the list. It also shows a project's details in a browser alert, formats dates for display, shows pop-up messages for three seconds, and starts a timer that reloads projects every 30 seconds.
sections.why: Likely reason: the confirmation prevents accidental deletes, and the timer keeps the list current without a manual refresh.
sections.watch_out: The 30 second timer starts when the page loads and is never stopped, so it keeps running for as long as the page stays open.

summary: A single web page that shows a dashboard, a list of solar projects with create and delete buttons, and a page of API links, all talking to the backend API.
purpose: Gives the owner a simple browser screen to see the project list, add a new project, remove one, and check whether the backend is reachable.
why: Likely reason: a plain page with no build step lets the app be opened in a browser directly, without a separate frontend project to compile.
how: The page loads Vue and Tailwind from the internet. On load, it checks the backend health route and fetches the project list. Each button calls a method that sends a request to the backend and then shows a short pop-up message. The project list refreshes every 30 seconds while the projects or dashboard tab is open.
inputs: Text typed into the new project form (name, asset type, location, capacity), button clicks, and the optional api address in the page URL or the window setting.
outputs: Requests to the backend for health, listing, creating, and deleting projects, plus visible tables, counts, status badges, and pop-up messages.
risks: If the backend returns an error body where a list is expected, the project list can be replaced with a non-list value and the page can break. The page also depends on two internet services, so it stops styling or working if they are unreachable. Deleting a project is permanent and relies only on a confirmation prompt.
debug: If the status badge says disconnected, check the backend address in the page setup, the ?api parameter, and whether the backend is running. If the list is empty or broken, open the browser developer console and look at the network response from the projects route. If the page is unstyled, check the internet access to the style and script hosts.
